A.explanation: An SI unit is useful but not essential, as non-SI units such as $\text{cm}$ or $\text{eV}$ can still record a valid measurement.

B.explanation: A physical quantity is defined by a numerical magnitude compared to a standard, so both a number and a unit are essential.

C.explanation: Derived SI units such as the newton or joule are acceptable, so the unit does not have to be a base unit.

D.explanation: Measurements can come from analogue or digital instruments, so an analogue scale is not essential.

hints: Notice the word essential in the question - ask what would make a recorded value like $5.2$ meaningless on its own.
Recall that a physical quantity expresses how many times a standard amount is contained in what is measured, which needs two parts.
Compare SI units, base units and analogue scales: they are all allowed choices, but ask whether any measurement could be valid without them.
walkthrough: Identify what the question asks: the minimum requirement for any recorded measurement of a physical quantity to have meaning.
State the physics rule: a physical quantity = numerical value $\times$ unit, for example $l = 2.5 \text{ m}$ needs both $2.5$ and $\text{m}$.
Check option A: SI units are standard but non-SI units are still valid measurements, so SI is not essential.
Check option C: many quantities use derived units such as $\text{N}$ or $\text{V}$, so a base unit such as $\text{kg}$ or $\text{m}$ is not essential.
Check option D: both digital balances and analogue rulers give valid measurements, so an analogue scale is not essential.
Conclude that only a number plus a unit is always required for the measurement to be understood. This is option B.
